Project overview

The problem

In public reviews, Nayatel customers complain less about a fault itself than about what happens after they report it: no clear status, visits that keep moving to "tomorrow", and explaining the same problem again.

What I designed

One flow inside the existing Support tab. It checks the connection, offers a short guided fix, sends a request already filled in, and tracks the visit until the customer confirms the result.

What isn't proven

The research is public reviews, not interviews, and the design hasn't been tested with users. It also assumes Nayatel can read line and router status remotely, which needs confirming.

  1. KnowSee whether the area, the line or the router is the likely problem.
  2. FixTry up to three safe steps, or skip them.
  3. RequestReview a request that's already filled in.
  4. Follow upTrack the visit and confirm the outcome.

Understanding the existing My Nayatel app

According to its store listing, My Nayatel already handles bills, usage, complaint launch and tracking, notifications and parental controls. A recent release added a Support module with lead time and ETA visibility. I wanted to add to that, not replace it.

  1. 1Support starts with a guess. The customer picks a category or a chip like "No Internet - WiFi" before anything about their connection is known.
  2. 2Status lives elsewhere. The Dashboard shows usage and billing, but nothing about whether the connection is working.
  3. 3The pieces exist. Complaint tracking and ETAs are already in the app, so the gap is connecting them, not inventing them.

Research and methodology

With no access to Nayatel's customers or data, I used what's public: 58 reviews and three news reports, collected on 22 October 2026. I read each review, tagged it with every theme it raised, and kept app problems separate from problems with the internet service itself. The appendix lists every review with its tags, so the counts below can be checked.

SourceWhat I readReviewsDates
Trustpilot, NayatelThe two most recent pages of reviews40Jan 2025 to Oct 2026
App Store, My NayatelAll reviews on the public reviews page102022 to 2026, some without a year
AppBrain, My NayatelReviews shown on the listing5Not shown
Google Play, My NayatelReviews shown in the listing preview3Not shown
NewsTechJuice, Bloom Pakistan, ProPakistani reports on outages–One from 2020; the others undated in my notes

Limits of this research

  • Review sites lean negative. People post when something goes wrong, so these reviews show where problems are, not how common they are.
  • 58 reviews is a small sample, and I couldn't verify any reviewer's account.
  • The sites only show some reviews. Google Play showed three in its preview, and Trustpilot's order affects which forty I read.
  • I tagged the reviews myself, with AI help for organising them, and nobody checked the tagging independently.
  • There were no interviews or usability tests. Everything about how customers feel is drawn from what they wrote.

Research findings and limitations

Four themes relate to the reporting journey. Counts are reviews that mention the theme, out of 58; one review can mention several.

Reporting a fault and then hearing nothing

18 of 58 · 12 about internet faults

The most common theme. Reviewers describe days without an update, complaints closed without a fix, and following up again and again.

"They'll keep on asking you for patience." AS-04

Not knowing when a technician will come

8 of 58

A visit promised for "tomorrow" day after day, a visit scheduled at 1 AM, and repeated visits that didn't fix the fault.

A visit scheduled "at 1:00 AM, a full 12 hours past the SLA". TP-28

Explaining the same problem again

6 of 58

Agents unaware of earlier contacts, being asked to brief a new person, and a dozen complaints for the same fault.

"I have already briefed the issue in detail and can't brief u again." TP-16

No clear explanation of the cause

4 of 58

Told to buy a new router, move it, or upgrade the package, with no explanation of what was actually wrong. This is the smallest theme, so the case for a connection check rests partly on my own interpretation.

What sits outside this project

ThemeReviewsHow I treated it

Installation, relocation and account requests17Out of scope. The same follow-up pattern shows up here, which suggests the tracking idea could extend later.
App reliability9A constraint. Crashes and a "unable to fetch data" error that blocked a complaint (AB-03) mean the new screens must stay light.
Billing and charges5Out of scope, except that unclear visit charges affect the request screen.
Positive experiences6One praised a staff member's clear follow-up after a long outage (AB-02). That's the experience this design tries to make routine.
Signals from Nayatel itself. These examples suggest that some of this information may already be available to Nayatel's support and operations teams. I couldn't establish whether it can be retrieved automatically for individual customers, so the diagnostic and outage features remain proposals that need technical validation.

Correction: an earlier draft of this case study estimated about 15 reviews about "is it me or Nayatel?". A full recount found 4, so I reframed the problem around follow-up, which the evidence supports more strongly.

Problem definition and design goals

When a home connection fails, a Nayatel customer can report it, but they can't see what's likely wrong or what's happening next. So they chase updates and repeat themselves.

How might we show customers what's likely wrong, and keep them informed from the moment they report it to the moment they confirm it's fixed?

Goals

  • Every wait shows a time.A restore estimate, a visit window or a "next update by" time, never an open-ended "soon".
  • Nothing is asked twice.The check result and the steps tried go into the request.
  • Simple faults get fixed without a visit.But only with steps that are safe for a customer to do.
  • The customer confirms the outcome.A request isn't resolved until they say it works.

Not in scope: connection speed, billing, installation, TV and the web version.

Proto-persona and user scenario

Illustrative user profile informed by review themes

  • Uses the home connection for work, freelancing or study TP-25 · TP-19
  • Shares it with a household that is also cut off AS-04
  • Follows up by phone, repeatedly, when nothing happens TP-28 · TP-36
  • Has been told to buy or move equipment without an explanation TP-21 · AB-04
  • Needs: a likely cause, a real time, and not having to start over
  • Assumed, not evidenced: isn't confident reading router lights

Zain's evening Fictional scenario

Zain is 21 and studies at a virtual university in Rawalpindi. At 7:40 PM, twenty minutes before a timed quiz, the home connection drops. He switches to mobile data and opens My Nayatel.

I use Zain to walk through the screens. His details are invented to make the scenario concrete; they aren't research findings.

Current versus proposed journey

Alternative solutions considered

OptionWhat it does wellWhy it falls short hereDecision
Conversational AI assistantFlexible; can answer questions outside a fixed flow.Reviewers already describe Nayatel's bots looping or failing to reach a person (TP-16, AS-03). A chat can't show a status at a glance, and it still needs the same diagnostic data underneath.Not chosen
Better complaint formCheapest to build; fits the current process.Improves the report but leaves the before and after untouched, which is where most complaints are.Not chosen
Guided check and trackingAdds the missing information before a report and keeps status visible after. Builds on the existing complaint tracking and ETAs.Depends on remote diagnostic data that I can't confirm exists.Chosen

A chat assistant could still sit on top of the chosen approach later. It would use the same check result instead of asking the customer to describe the problem.

Design principles and rationale

  • Say what we know, and how sure we are

    The check says "most likely" rather than "the cause is", and shows when it ran and what it was based on. A wrong diagnosis stated as fact would repeat the problem in the reviews.

  • Carry information forward

    The check result and the steps tried move into the request automatically, and the customer can still edit them. This answers the re-explaining theme directly.

  • Give every wait a time and a source

    Restore estimates, visit windows and "next update by" times each come with when they were last updated.

  • Never make a step a gate

    Every troubleshooting step can be skipped, and reporting is always one tap away. Someone uncomfortable touching equipment shouldn't be stuck.

  • Let the customer close the loop

    A request is resolved only when the customer says it works. "Still not working" reopens it without re-entering anything.

User flow and decision points

  1. 1. What did the check find?Router or line issue leads to the guided fix. An area outage shows a restore estimate and ends the flow. A failed check offers a retry or a report without a check.
  2. 2. Did the fix work?"Fixed" re-checks and ends. "Still not working" or skipping moves on, and after the last step goes to the request.
  3. 3. Is it working after the visit?"Yes" leads to an optional rating and closes the request. "Still not working" reopens it.

Wireframes and iterations

I kept the wireframes greyscale so reviews stayed on structure and wording. A problem is shown by shape and weight only, so the faulty part of the check is the one dark cell.

From wireframe to hi-fi

Connection check

  • Moved from Home into its own screen, opened from Support, so existing screens stay untouched.
  • The three parts became a path "from Nayatel to your home", one row per hop.
  • The verdict now says "most likely" and the footer says what the check was based on.

Request

  • Slots are labelled as requested times; the exact visit is confirmed later.
  • Added a notes field and an optional photo of the router lights.
  • "Already tried" stays editable, and items can be removed.

Resolution

  • The question became "Is your internet working again?" with "Yes" and "Still not working", the same words as the guided fix.
  • The rating only appears after a yes.
  • Reopening no longer promises the same technician.

What changed after the wireframe critique

  • Confirm before ratingThe first version asked for stars with "Yes" already selected.
  • Equal weight for "Fixed" and "Still not working"One dark button nudged people toward a complaint.
  • One main action, always at the bottomThe main button had moved between cards and footers.
  • Fewer text sizes, bigger targetsAbout 14 sizes became 6, and every tap target became at least 44px.

Visual design system

Someone whose internet has just dropped shouldn't feel they've left the app they know. So I didn't create a new look. I sampled the existing app's navy cards, orange actions, pale blue background and Roboto type from screenshots, and built each new component from those parts.

Orange means "do this"

Only the next action is orange. Selected and structural elements are navy.

No alarm red

Faults are amber with a plain word. Red would add panic to a moment that's already stressful.

Words before colour

Every status has a word and an icon, so it still reads for colour-blind users and in bright sunlight.

Final screens and interactive prototype

Entry

The Dashboard doesn't change. Support gets a Connection health card.

Know

The check runs on Nayatel's side and answers in one sentence, with when and how it checked.

Fix

Three steps a customer can do safely. The fibre step only asks them to look, never to unplug.

Request

Filled in from the check, editable, with requested times rather than bookings.

Follow up

Assigned, on the way, arrived. Late arrivals and reschedules show the new time and when it changed.

Close the loop

The customer confirms, rates if they want to, or reopens.

Roman Urdu

I included Roman Urdu as an additional language option to explore, based on my own design assumption. Its usefulness and preferred language format would need to be tested with Nayatel subscribers.

Key design decisions and trade-offs

  • Add to Support instead of redesigning Home

    People with a problem already go to Support, and leaving existing screens alone makes this easier to ship.

    Trade-off: one tap further away. The Dashboard's "Launch Complaint" leads there, which helps.

  • Fill in the request from the check

    The check result and the steps tried go into the request, answering the re-explaining theme.

    Trade-off: it relies on remote diagnostics, so the request also works when the check fails.

  • Requested times, not bookings

    The customer requests a time; the exact visit is confirmed once a technician is assigned.

    Trade-off: less certain up front, but it doesn't promise what dispatch may not be able to keep.

  • End the flow during an outage

    If the area is down, the app says so with an estimate and offers to notify. There's nothing to fix or report.

    Trade-off: estimates can slip, so each one shows when it was updated and when the next update is due.

  • The customer closes the request

    A visit counts as resolved only when the customer says it works.

    Trade-off: some requests stay open longer, because they weren't really fixed.

Edge cases and error states

The happy path is the easy part. These are the cases where trust is won or lost. Where the right behaviour depends on Nayatel's operations, I've marked it as a proposal.

  • The check service is unavailable

    In the prototype

    Says the check couldn't finish and that this doesn't mean anything is wrong. Offers a retry, or a report without a check that tells the technician to start from the beginning.

  • Outage with no restore estimate

    In the prototype

    Shows "Not known yet" instead of a guessed time, and still gives a "next update by" time.

  • The restore estimate changes

    In the prototype

    Shows the new time with the old one crossed out, and when it was updated.

  • The outage is fixed but the customer is still offline

    In the prototype

    Says the area is back, marks the line and router as not checked yet, and runs the check on those.

  • The customer can't or won't do a step

    In the prototype

    Every step can be skipped and "Report a problem" is always there. Skipped steps are recorded as skipped, not as tried.

  • The technician misses the window

    In the prototype Rest proposed

    A "Running late" state shows the revised window and when it changed. What happens after a no-show, and whether the customer gets an option to rebook, depends on dispatch policy, so I haven't designed it.

  • No mobile data

    Proposed, needs validation

    The app can't run the check without some connection. A possible fallback is an SMS with the area status, or the last check result kept on the phone. Both depend on systems I can't see.

    Not designed

  • The customer doesn't confirm

    Proposed, needs validation

    One reminder, then close the request with a note that it can be reopened. How long to wait is a policy decision for Nayatel, not something I should set.

    Not designed

Proposed success metrics and validation

This is a concept with no live data, so there are no results to report. If it shipped, I'd watch these, comparing against the current flow.

MetricWhy it matters
Follow-up calls per requestThe clearest test of whether status updates replace chasing.
Repeat requests for the same faultWhether customers stop starting over.
Share of checks ending in "Fixed"How many visits the guided fix avoids. Watch it alongside reopen rates, so it isn't hiding unsolved faults.
Helpline calls during a known outageWhether the outage notice reaches people in the app.
Requests reopened after "resolved"How often a visit closes without a real fix.

How I'd validate it before building

  • Five or six moderated sessions with subscribers who rely on home internet, using the prototype. Tasks: find out what's wrong, follow the fibre step, send a request, react to a late technician.
  • A wording test on the verdicts: do people read "most likely your router" as a guess or a fact?
  • Watch whether people can follow the router steps with their own equipment, since models differ.
  • Ask Nayatel's engineers what can be read remotely before any visual design goes further.

Technical considerations and design handoff

I don't know what Nayatel's systems can do. Every row below needs confirming with engineering before this design is more than a proposal.

The design needsProbably comes fromOpen question
Area outage status and restore estimateNetwork operations outage recordsCan an estimate be shared per area, and how often does it update?
Fibre line statusLine monitoring for the customer's connectionIs a fault like LOS visible remotely, per customer?
Router reachabilityRemote router management, if supportedWhich router models can be reached, and how quickly?
Visit times and confirmationThe existing complaint system and Support moduleCan the app offer requested windows and confirm one later?
Technician status and nameField dispatchAre "left", "arrived" and "late" events recorded in real time?

What a developer would get

  • Each component with its states, as listed in the visual system section.
  • Colour, type, spacing and radius tokens, documented in the project's DESIGN.md.
  • All copy in English and Roman Urdu, kept in one string table in the prototype.
  • A direct link to every state in the prototype, for review and QA.
  • The open questions above, so build estimates start from the right assumptions.

How I used AI

Where AI helped

  • Collecting public reviews and organising my tags
  • Drafting wireframe and prototype code to my direction
  • Critiquing layouts and listing edge cases to consider
  • Tightening copy and drafting the Roman Urdu strings

What I decided

  • The scope: one connected flow instead of many screens
  • The online student scenario, and Roman Urdu over Urdu script
  • Matching the existing app rather than a new visual identity
  • Which critique points to accept, and re-checking the research when the numbers didn't hold up

AI didn't interview anyone, run usability tests or validate this design. Those are the next steps.

Reflection and next steps

The research changed my framing. I started from "customers can't tell whose fault it is", but the reviews say more about what happens after reporting. The check is still useful, but the tracking and the "never ask twice" request are what the evidence supports most.

If I continued, I'd validate the data first, test the verdict wording and the router steps with real subscribers, then look at Urdu script, the web version and a screen-reader audit.
